Thank you for submitting your work entitled "Quantitative mapping of protein-peptide affinity landscapes using spectrally encoded beads" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by two peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and a Senior Editor. The following individual involved in review of your submission has agreed to reveal his identity: Toby Gibson (Reviewer #2).

Our decision has been reached after consultation within the editorial board. Based on these discussions and the individual reviews below, we regret to inform you that your work will not be considered further for publication in eLife. In particular, there was uniform agreement that the issues raised by reviewer 1 are highly unlikely to be addressed in revision.

Reviewer #1:

In this study, the authors present a new technique to measure the affinity of protein-peptide interaction in parallel. They apply their method to the well-known Calcineurin-PxIxIT interaction, obtain more data on this interaction, and use it to identify high-affinity peptides. They validate some of these peptides in a cell-based assay.

This work is based around the bead-encoded peptide-synthesis and subsequent affinity measurements using the spectral encoding. This all strikes me as technically state-of-the-art and quite elegant. However, from the paper as written, it is a bit difficult to get a true sense of the advantages of the new method over existing ones, and no direct comparison is attempted in the manuscript. For instance, mapping of the affinities of substitutions (as in Figure 4) surely would be possible using SPOT (to a slightly different degree, also using Phage). The shown r2 of 0.68 is pretty good, but not all that much higher than what has been claimed for SPOT (though a little higher than for phage – see e.g., Ivarsson et al., where, of course, a much higher number of peptides is measured). One should also note that this is for the same protein – incidentally, modern computational methods (such as alchemy-based ones, e.g., TI or CGI) achieve these sort of correlations, and usually perform better than rosetta. As high-quality structures are available, they would be applicable in this case, and may perform similar to the new bead-based method.

Similar things hold for the high-affinity variants obtained here (Figure 5 or later). While obtaining low-nanomolar binding peptides is really quite good, this domain is (as the authors themselves state) what phage display really is optimized for. While their new method can incorporate non-canonical amino acids, that is similarly true of novel synthetic library methods as what recently came out of the Pentelute lab.

Finally, while the authors seem to emphasize ability to detect "weak" affinities, I only see convincing data for affinities of up to maybe 50uM, which is all still detectable using techniques such as AP-MS or phage.

I should note that I do not really want to sound too negative. I see a new technique that brings substantial technical innovation that could be very exciting in this field. However, I find it difficult to ascertain its advantages over the variety of existing methods in the manuscript as presented. I would strongly suggest to include more direct comparisons with existing methods (such as SPOT, ProP-PD, hold-up, etc.) as well a more detailed discussion thereof.

A few additional points:

1) The authors state "CN binds PxIxIT peptides with weak affinities.… estimates for known substrates have varied over a wide range.…". These statements are somewhat contradictory in itself and, in any case, the affinities listed in Figure 2A seem to be all in the single digit uM, which is neither a wide range, nor particularly weak (roughly the expected range for domain-motif interactions).

2) Given the relatively length of the current paper, it would be good scholarship to discuss existing methods (including the variety of phage-display approaches, SPOT arrays and the recently developed holdup assay) – currently, this all happens in part of a single paragraph, with some of the methods I point out above not even mentioned.

3) In a similar vein, the citations (or lack thereof) are a bit puzzling. A 12-year old paper (Neduva and Russell) is cited regarding motif-interactions in Y2H/AP-MS, when most of the relevant work was published in the last decade. For Proteomic phage display, only a review paper is cited.

Reviewer #2:

This paper introduces MRBLE-pep, a medium-scale throughput protein-peptide affinity tool and applies it to calcineurin and variants of the PxIxIT docking motif. Using MRBLEs – colour-coded microbeads, each position in the original peptide can be substituted with all other amino acids. Systematic evaluation of binding determinants can then be rapidly determined using small amounts of reagents. Efficient methods for examining SLiM specificities are vey much needed given the abundance of protein:motif interactions in cell regulation and therefore MRBLE could see widespread adoption. Although the PxIxIT motif is well known from several calcineurin substrates, there has been uncertainty regarding the motif specificity determinants as well as the cooperative involvement of the second LxVP docking motif.

Weight matrices (PSSMs/HMMs) are often used to represent SLiMs in sequence searches but assume that each position in the sequence can be treated independently of the others. Regular expressions are also in widespread use but are overdetermined and insufficiently flexible regarding sequence space. The results here can be used to improve bioinformatic PxIxIT detection in candidate substrate proteins. However, the results also emphasise that positions in the PxIxIT motif are not independent and also that flanking residues affect the binding affinity (which has been seen for a number of other linear motifs too). The data from MRBLE-pep could allow a different computational approach whereby candidate motifs in protein sequences could be compared to and ranked by the total landscape affinity data.

No substantive concerns were identified.

[Editors’ note: what now follows is the decision letter after the authors submitted for further consideration.]

Thank you for resubmitting your work entitled "Quantitative mapping of protein-peptide affinity landscapes using spectrally encoded beads" for further consideration at eLife. Your article has been reviewed by two peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and a Senior Editor.

The manuscript has been improved but there are some remaining issues that need to be addressed before acceptance, as outlined below in the first review below. Normally, we try to avoid second revisions, but we feel reviewer #1's comments should be addressed and we hope you will be able to do this easily and quickly.

Reviewer #1:

Essentially, the revisions by the authors haven't changed my opinions drastically. I still see this is as an innovative technology that will likely be of interest; however, the paper is still hampered by some shortcomings that I think could be improved pretty easily. In a way I find it a bit frustrating that the authors choose to write a full two pages of rebuttal to a simple point (correlations to measured affinity - compare these R2s between SPOT and MRBLE-pep) when they could have simply provided two numbers. Also, little of these two pages of rebuttal seems to have made it to the text (or was in there to begin with). Why not provide some kind of comparison of correlation to measured affinity to SPOT in the paper? I'm reasonably certain MRBLE-pep would come out on top.

Similarly, the authors add calculations using FoldX (that I didn't ask for). Not sure why they include comparisons of FoldX to Rosetta in the main text/figure (these would be of interest in computational papers and indeed have been done a bit, but I doubt the main readership of this paper will be interested). Also, I find it a bit frustrating that while they added a many new figures, the one figure that I think would have added to the paper (again a simple direct comparison of ddGs derived from MRBLE-pep to ones derived from rosetta OR FoldX vs. measured ddGs, i.e. combining the panels of Figure 4—figure supplement 4 into one panel and comparing it to the appropriate one for MRLBLE-pep). It's fine if the authors don't want to do any TI/FEP calculations (again, this isn't a computational paper), though if they do want to make the point that FoldX/Rosetta don't perform well on solvent exposed residues (not surprising), they should also mention that this is something that TI/FEP would, at least in theory, do better at.

They did add a much more appropriate introduction with discussion of the literature.

Reviewer #2:

The original MRBLE-pep manuscript was rather let down by superficial treatment of other PPI methods and how MARBL-pep compares to them. The resubmitted manuscript is greatly improved in this regard. This is important because SLiM researchers need to be able to understand which methods are suitable for the projects they have in mind. These range from the low throughput "gold standard" ITC up to whole proteome screens of the "disorderome" with phage display to identify novel SLiM candidates. I believe that MARBL-pep will see significant adoption and will help to define many SLiM motif patterns. The data obtained for the chosen target, the Calcineurin-binding PxIxIT motif, will hopefully now be applied in the identification of novel substrates for this medically important phosphatase. I have no further concerns.

claims.claim: Nearly 40% of protein-protein interactions are mediated by 3–10 amino acid Short Linear Motifs (SLiMs) interacting with protein globular domains or enzymes.
claims.source: Nearly 40% of these interactions are mediated by 3–10 amino acid Short Linear Motifs (SLiMs) interacting with protein globular domains (e.g. SH3, SH2, and PDZ domains) or enzymes (e.g. kinases and phosphatases) (Dinkel et al., 2016; Neduva and Russell, 2006; Tompa et al., 2014).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Dinkel et al., 2016; Neduva and Russell, 2006; Tompa et al., 2014).

claims.claim: The human proteome is estimated to contain more than 100,000 SLiMs.
claims.source: The human proteome is estimated to contain more than 100,000 of these SLiMs, many of which are highly regulated by post-translational modifications (PTMs) such as phosphorylation (Tompa et al., 2014; Ivarsson and Jemth, 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Tompa et al., 2014; Ivarsson and Jemth, 2019).

claims.claim: Many SLiMs are highly regulated by post-translational modifications such as phosphorylation.
claims.source: The human proteome is estimated to contain more than 100,000 of these SLiMs, many of which are highly regulated by post-translational modifications (PTMs) such as phosphorylation (Tompa et al., 2014; Ivarsson and Jemth, 2019).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Tompa et al., 2014; Ivarsson and Jemth, 2019).

claims.claim: Calcineurin is a conserved Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent phosphatase.
claims.source: Calcineurin (CN), a conserved Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent phosphatase, is a prime example of a signaling protein that relies on weak SLiM-mediated interactions for substrate recognition.
claims.evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about calcineurin.

claims.claim: Calcineurin plays critical roles in the human immune, nervous, and cardiovascular systems.
claims.source: Although CN plays critical roles in the human immune, nervous, and cardiovascular systems and likely dephosphorylates hundreds of downstream targets, only ∼70 are known to date (Sheftic et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Sheftic et al., 2016).

claims.claim: Calcineurin likely dephosphorylates hundreds of downstream targets, but only ∼70 are known to date.
claims.source: Although CN plays critical roles in the human immune, nervous, and cardiovascular systems and likely dephosphorylates hundreds of downstream targets, only ∼70 are known to date (Sheftic et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Sheftic et al., 2016).

claims.claim: Dephosphorylation of NFAT by calcineurin is required for T-cell activation and adaptive immunity.
claims.source: These include the NFAT family of transcription factors, whose dephosphorylation by CN is required for T-cell activation and adaptive immunity (Jain et al., 1993).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Jain et al., 1993).

claims.claim: Calcineurin is the target of the widely used immunosuppressants cyclosporin A (CysA) and FK506.
claims.source: Consequently, CN is the target of the widely used immunosuppressants cyclosporin A (CysA) and FK506.
claims.evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about calcineurin inhibitors.

claims.claim: Calcineurin recognizes substrates by binding to two characterized SLiMs (PxIxIT and LxVP) located at variable distances from the phosphosite.
claims.source: CN dephosphorylates sites with little sequence similarity, instead recognizing substrates by binding to two characterized SLiMs (PxIxIT and LxVP) located at variable distances from the phosphosite (Roy and Cyert, 2009).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Roy and Cyert, 2009).

claims.claim: FK506 and CysA prevent LxVP docking to calcineurin.
claims.source: Blocking SLiM binding to CN prevents dephosphorylation without altering its catalytic center: FK506 and CysA prevent LxVP docking, the viral inhibitor A238L blocks PxIxIT and LxVP binding, and the high-affinity peptide inhibitor PVIVIT blocks PxIxIT binding (Grigoriu et al., 2013; Aramburu et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Grigoriu et al., 2013; Aramburu et al., 1999).

claims.claim: The viral inhibitor A238L blocks PxIxIT and LxVP binding to calcineurin.
claims.source: Blocking SLiM binding to CN prevents dephosphorylation without altering its catalytic center: FK506 and CysA prevent LxVP docking, the viral inhibitor A238L blocks PxIxIT and LxVP binding, and the high-affinity peptide inhibitor PVIVIT blocks PxIxIT binding (Grigoriu et al., 2013; Aramburu et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Grigoriu et al., 2013; Aramburu et al., 1999).

claims.claim: The high-affinity peptide inhibitor PVIVIT blocks PxIxIT binding to calcineurin.
claims.source: Blocking SLiM binding to CN prevents dephosphorylation without altering its catalytic center: FK506 and CysA prevent LxVP docking, the viral inhibitor A238L blocks PxIxIT and LxVP binding, and the high-affinity peptide inhibitor PVIVIT blocks PxIxIT binding (Grigoriu et al., 2013; Aramburu et al., 1999).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Grigoriu et al., 2013; Aramburu et al., 1999).

claims.claim: The affinities of PxIxIT motifs determine biological output by specifying the Ca2+ concentration-dependence of substrate dephosphorylation in vivo.
claims.source: The affinities of PxIxIT motifs determine biological output by specifying the Ca2+ concentration-dependence of substrate dephosphorylation in vivo (Müller et al., 2009; Roy et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Müller et al., 2009; Roy et al., 2007).

claims.claim: The relationship between PxIxIT sequence and CN binding affinity has never been probed outside of the core motif.
claims.source: However, the relationship between PxIxIT sequence and CN binding affinity has never been probed outside of the core motif.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this work.

claims.claim: Display-based methods such as combinatorial phage display and ProP-PD allow screening for binding between a protein of interest and large libraries (up to 10^10) of candidate SLiM-containing peptides.
claims.source: Display-based methods such as combinatorial phage display (Tonikian et al., 2008) and ProP-PD (Ivarsson et al., 2014; Sundell and Ivarsson, 2014) allow screening for binding between a protein of interest and large libraries (up to 1010) of candidate SLiM-containing peptides.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Tonikian et al., 2008; Ivarsson et al., 2014; Sundell and Ivarsson, 2014).

claims.claim: Display-based methods typically identify only strong binders and cannot return negative information about residues that ablate binding.
claims.source: However, these methods typically identify only strong binders, cannot return negative information about residues that ablate binding critical for downstream target prediction in vivo (Gfeller et al., 2011), and do not directly probe effects of PTMs.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to published literature (Gfeller et al., 2011).

claims.claim: Display-based methods do not directly probe effects of PTMs.
claims.source: However, these methods typically identify only strong binders, cannot return negative information about residues that ablate binding critical for downstream target prediction in vivo (Gfeller et al., 2011), and do not directly probe effects of PTMs.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of display-based methods.

claims.claim: Array-based methods allow quantification of binding of labeled proteins to 10s-100s (SPOT arrays), tens of thousands, or millions (ultra-high density arrays) of peptides chemically synthesized in situ.
claims.source: Array-based methods (Fodor et al., 1991) allow quantification of binding of labeled proteins to 10s-100s (SPOT arrays) (Frank et al., 1990), tens of thousands (Atwater et al., 2018), or millions (ultra-high density arrays) (Buus et al., 2012; Forsström et al., 2014; Price et al., 2012; Carmona et al., 2015) of peptides chemically synthesized in situ, permitting direct incorporation of PTMs or unnatural amino acids at specific positions (Engelmann et al., 2014; Tinti et al., 2013; Filippakopoulos et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Fodor et al., 1991; Frank et al., 1990; Atwater et al., 2018; Buus et al., 2012; Forsström et al., 2014; Price et al., 2012; Carmona et al., 2015; Engelmann et al., 2014; Tinti et al., 2013; Filippakopoulos et al., 2012).

claims.claim: Array-based methods permit direct incorporation of PTMs or unnatural amino acids at specific positions.
claims.source: Array-based methods (Fodor et al., 1991) allow quantification of binding of labeled proteins to 10s-100s (SPOT arrays) (Frank et al., 1990), tens of thousands (Atwater et al., 2018), or millions (ultra-high density arrays) (Buus et al., 2012; Forsström et al., 2014; Price et al., 2012; Carmona et al., 2015) of peptides chemically synthesized in situ, permitting direct incorporation of PTMs or unnatural amino acids at specific positions (Engelmann et al., 2014; Tinti et al., 2013; Filippakopoulos et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Engelmann et al., 2014; Tinti et al., 2013; Filippakopoulos et al., 2012).

claims.claim: It is difficult to evaluate the yield and purity of peptides in each spot of array-based methods, contributing to false positives and negatives.
claims.source: However, it is difficult to evaluate the yield and purity of peptides in each spot, contributing to false positives and negatives (Tinti et al., 2013; Blikstad and Ivarsson, 2015).
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Tinti et al., 2013; Blikstad and Ivarsson, 2015).

claims.claim: Peptides are synthesized directly on spectrally encoded beads (MRBLEs) with a unique linkage between each peptide sequence and a given spectral code.
claims.source: Peptides are synthesized directly on spectrally encoded beads (MRBLEs, Microspheres with Ratiometric Barcode Lanthanide Encoding) (Gerver et al., 2012; Nguyen et al., 2017a) with a unique linkage between each peptide sequence and a given spectral code.
claims.evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Gerver et al., 2012; Nguyen et al., 2017a) and describes the MRBLE-pep method.

claims.claim: On-MRBLE chemical synthesis allows for precise control of peptide density, incorporation of PTMs at known locations, and in-line assessment of peptide quality via mass spectrometry.
claims.source: On-MRBLE chemical synthesis allows for precise control of peptide density, incorporation of PTMs at known locations, and in-line assessment of peptide quality via mass spectrometry to identify amino acids that ablate and promote protein binding with equal confidence.
claims.evidence: This describes capabilities of the MRBLE-pep method developed in this work.

claims.claim: MRBLE polymeric beads have been deliberately engineered to have slow on- and off-rates, thereby slowing dissociation and allowing quantitative measurement of weak and transient interactions.
claims.source: Most importantly, MRBLE polymeric beads have been deliberately engineered to have slow on- and off-rates, thereby slowing dissociation and allowing quantitative measurement interaction strengths for of weak and transient interactions difficult to detect via other techniques.
claims.evidence: This describes a key feature of the MRBLE-pep method developed in this work.

claims.claim: Flanking amino acids and post-translational modifications play critical and previously unappreciated roles in determining PxIxIT-CN affinity and specificity.
claims.source: We find that flanking amino acids and post-translational modifications play surprisingly critical and previously unappreciated roles in determining affinity and specificity.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claims.claim: Several PxIxIT peptides with unprecedented binding affinity to calcineurin were identified.
claims.source: Through iterative cycles of mutagenesis, in vitro affinity measurements, and in vivo activity measurements, we map the CN-PxIxIT affinity landscape and identify several PxIxIT peptides of unprecedented binding affinity that could prove useful for future development of additional potent CN inhibitors.
claims.evidence: This is a primary finding of the study based on experimental data.

claims.claim: MRBLEs containing a given code are output to a filtered-tip in a 96-well format or two 48–2 mL reaction tubes.
claims.source: MRBLEs containing a given code are output to a filtered-tip in a 96-well format or two 48–2 mL reaction tubes (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: This describes the experimental method and is illustrated in Figure 1A.

claims.claim: Spectral codes can be 'read' using a single UV excitation source, preserving the ability to multiplex binding measurements using up to three detection antibodies.
claims.source: Unlike commercially available spectrally encoded beads (e.g. Luminex), spectral codes can be 'read' using a single UV excitation source, preserving the ability to multiplex binding measurements using up to three detection antibodies (Nguyen et al., 2017b).
claims.evidence: This describes a feature of the MRBLE-pep method and is supported by a citation (Nguyen et al., 2017b).

claims.claim: Measured MRBLE lanthanide ratios before, during, and after SPPS remained constant.
claims.source: Measured MRBLE lanthanide ratios before, during, and after SPPS remained constant, (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), establishing that embedded codes are unchanged by chemical exposures.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Bound DyLight650-SA intensities saturated at ∼20 nM DyLight650-SA for ∼7100 beads in a 100 μL reaction volume, establishing a surface density of ∼2 × 10^8 peptide molecules per MRBLE.
claims.source: Bound DyLight650-SA intensities were relatively consistent between sequences (Figure 1—figure supplement 3) and saturated at ∼20 nM DyLight650-SA for ∼7100 beads in a 100 μL reaction volume (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), establishing a surface density of ∼2 × 108 peptide molecules per MRBLE.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental measurement shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claims.claim: Prior literature affinity estimates for a given substrate have varied over 50-fold (NFATc1 and RCAN1).
claims.source: Measuring CN-PxIxIT binding affinities represents a demanding test for a new protein-peptide interaction assay, as CN binds PxIxIT peptide with moderate-to-weak affinities (Figure 2A) via surface interactions (Figure 2B), and prior literature affinity estimates for a given substrate have varied over 50-fold (Figure 2A, NFATc1 and RCAN1).
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the state of the literature, illustrated in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: The high-affinity PVIVIT and PVIVVT variants showed strong binding to calcineurin.
claims.source: Consistent with previous observations, the high-affinity PVIVIT and PVIVVT variants showed strong binding, a scrambled peptide showed no binding, and the PVIAVT and PVIVIN variants showed low to intermediate binding (Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 1), with consistent results for the same peptide sequence synthesized on MRBLEs with different codes.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: A scrambled peptide showed no binding to calcineurin.
claims.source: Consistent with previous observations, the high-affinity PVIVIT and PVIVVT variants showed strong binding, a scrambled peptide showed no binding, and the PVIAVT and PVIVIN variants showed low to intermediate binding (Figure 2C, Figure 2—source data 1), with consistent results for the same peptide sequence synthesized on MRBLEs with different codes.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: MALDI mass spectrometry confirmed successful synthesis of both RCAN1 and NFATc1 full-length peptides.
claims.source: Although MALDI mass spectrometry confirmed successful synthesis of both RCAN1 and NFATc1 full-length peptides, binding was near the limit of detection in this assay (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation using MALDI mass spectrometry.

claims.claim: RCAN1 and NFATc1 binding to calcineurin was near the limit of detection in the MRBLE-pep assay.
claims.source: Although MALDI mass spectrometry confirmed successful synthesis of both RCAN1 and NFATc1 full-length peptides, binding was near the limit of detection in this assay (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 2C.

claims.claim: The PKIVIT peptide binds slightly more strongly than PVIVIT to calcineurin.
claims.source: These data reproduce previously observed trends and additionally suggest that the PKIVIT peptide binds slightly more strongly than PVIVIT; therefore, we also selected PKIVIT for additional systematic mutagenesis.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation from the MRBLE-pep assay.

claims.claim: Measured intensities for MRBLE-pep appear to saturate at 5–6 hr and decrease only slightly after 24 hr.
claims.source: Intensities appear to saturate at 5–6 hr and decrease only slightly after 24 hr. Pink boxes signify the time window for all subsequent measurements.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: MRBLEs were specifically engineered to have very slow on- and off-rates (with measured rates on the order of hours).
claims.source: Although these measurements take place out of equilibrium due to the need to wash beads prior to imaging, we specifically engineered MRBLEs to have very slow on- and off-rates (with measured rates on the order of hours) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—figure supplement 2), allowing measured intensities to approximate equilibrium values to yield apparent dissociation constants (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: This is a design feature of the method, supported by experimental data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Slow on- and off-rates have previously been observed for hydrogel particles and are known to scale with particle radius.
claims.source: Slow on- and off-rates have previously been observed for hydrogel particles and are known to scale with particle radius, as proteins initially encounter and bind bead-bound ligands and then slowly diffuse into the particle via iterative dissociation and rebinding events (Shapiro et al., 2012).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature (Shapiro et al., 2012).

claims.claim: Examination of known CN PxIxIT motifs suggested a potential preference for positively charged (R, K) or hydroxyl (S) residues in the degenerate PxIxIT position 2.
claims.source: Examination of known CN PxIxIT motifs (NFATc1, NFATc2) and a viral inhibitor (A238L) suggested a potential preference for positively charged (R, K) or hydroxyl (S) residues in the degenerate PxIxIT position 2 (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 2A.

claims.claim: All mutations away from the native residue at position 2 in NFATc2 resulted in a dramatic loss of binding.
claims.source: While the experiments presented here did not directly test the functional consequences of a R2Q mutation, all mutations away from the native residue at this position resulted in a dramatic loss of binding (Figure 3—figure supplement 17), and the P7A substitution led to a nearly complete loss of binding (Figure 3—figure supplement 6, Figure 3—figure supplement 17, Figure 3—figure supplement 18).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 17.

claims.claim: The P7A substitution in NFATc2 led to a nearly complete loss of binding to calcineurin.
claims.source: While the experiments presented here did not directly test the functional consequences of a R2Q mutation, all mutations away from the native residue at this position resulted in a dramatic loss of binding (Figure 3—figure supplement 17), and the P7A substitution led to a nearly complete loss of binding (Figure 3—figure supplement 6, Figure 3—figure supplement 17, Figure 3—figure supplement 18).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6, Figure 3—figure supplement 17, and Figure 3—figure supplement 18.

claims.claim: Many substitutions at positions 2 and 4 had unexpectedly strong effects on binding to calcineurin.
claims.source: Although considered to be degenerate in the consensus motif, many substitutions at positions 2 and 4 had unexpectedly strong effects on binding (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: V2R and V2K mutations in the PVIVIT scaffold significantly enhanced binding to calcineurin.
claims.source: In particular, V2R and V2K mutations in the PVIVIT scaffold significantly enhanced binding in experimental assays, consistent with previous observations of high-affinity CN binding to the viral inhibitor (A238L) containing a positively-charged residue at this position (PKIIIT) (Grigoriu et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation consistent with published literature (Grigoriu et al., 2013).

claims.claim: The experimental impact of sequences flanking the core 'PxIxIT' residues on CN binding has never been probed systematically.
claims.source: The experimental impact of sequences flanking the core 'PxIxIT' residues on CN binding has never been probed systematically.
claims.evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this work.

claims.claim: At the −1 position, MRBLE-pep data revealed a clear CN preference for hydrophobic residues (V,L,I) and a weak preference for polar residues (T, Y, H, N, and R) for all three of the PVIVIT, PKIVIT, and NFATc2 scaffolds.
claims.source: At the −1 position, MRBLE-pep data revealed a clear CN preference for hydrophobic residues (V,L,I) and a weak preference for polar residues (T, Y, H, N, and R) for all three of the PVIVIT, PKIVIT, and NFATc2 scaffolds.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental finding from the MRBLE-pep assay.

claims.claim: Substitution to acidic (D, E) residues at position −1 strongly reduced binding to calcineurin.
claims.source: By contrast, substitution to acidic (D, E) residues at this position strongly reduced binding (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1, Figure 3—figure supplement 2, Figure 3—figure supplement 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 4, Figure 3—figure supplement 5, Figure 3—figure supplement 6, Figure 3—figure supplement 13, Figure 3—figure supplement 14, Figure 3—figure supplement 15, Figure 3—figure supplement 16, Figure 3—figure supplement 17, Figure 3—figure supplement 18).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in multiple figures.

claims.claim: The effect of phosphoserine and phosphothreonine at position 9 was specific to the PVIVIT sequence, with significantly less drastic increases and decreases in affinity observed for the same substitutions in the NFATc2 and AKAP79 scaffolds.
claims.source: This effect was specific to the PVIVIT sequence, with significantly less drastic increases and decreases in affinity observed for the same substitutions in the NFATc2 and AKAP79 scaffolds, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 6, Figure 3—figure supplement 8, Figure 3—figure supplement 23).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 6, Figure 3—figure supplement 8, and Figure 3—figure supplement 23.

claims.claim: MRBLE-pep data establish that flanking residues make major contributions to affinity and the PxIxIT SLiM is significantly longer than previously thought.
claims.source: These MRBLE-pep data establish that flanking residues make major contributions to affinity and the PxIxIT SLiM is significantly longer than previously thought.
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on experimental data from the MRBLE-pep assay.

claims.claim: The V4F substitution resulted in a significant loss of affinity within the PVIVIT context but had only minor effects on PKIVIT binding.
claims.source: DMC analysis between the PVIVIT and PKIVIT scaffolds revealed that the V4F substitution resulted in a significant loss of affinity within the PVIVIT context but had only minor effects on PKIVIT binding; by contrast, V4I mutation of this solvent-exposed position significantly increased binding only within the PKIVIT sequence (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 23).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation from double-mutant cycle analysis shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 23.

claims.claim: V4I mutation significantly increased binding only within the PKIVIT sequence.
claims.source: DMC analysis between the PVIVIT and PKIVIT scaffolds revealed that the V4F substitution resulted in a significant loss of affinity within the PVIVIT context but had only minor effects on PKIVIT binding; by contrast, V4I mutation of this solvent-exposed position significantly increased binding only within the PKIVIT sequence (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 23).
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation from double-mutant cycle analysis shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 23.

claims.claim: The high affinity of the PKIIIT sequence in the A238L inhibitor relies on cooperativity between the position 2 and 4 residues.
claims.source: This last substitution suggests that the high affinity of the PKIIIT sequence in the A238L inhibitor in particular relies on cooperativity between the position 2 and 4 residues.
claims.evidence: This is an inference based on experimental observations.

claims.claim: Co-crystal structures of CN bound to PVIVIT and AKAP79-derived PIAIIIT reveal that the conserved P1, I3, and I5 residues are buried in hydrophobic pockets on the CN surface.
claims.source: Co-crystal structures of CN bound to PVIVIT (PDB: 2P6B) (Li et al., 2007) and AKAP79-derived PIAIIIT (PDB: 3LL8) (Li et al., 2012) reveal that the conserved P1, I3, and I5 residues are buried in hydrophobic pockets on the CN surface in all three structures; for AKAP79, an I1 residue occupies the pocket typically occupied by a P1 residue.
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of published crystal structures (PDB: 2P6B and 3LL8) cited in the text (Li et al., 2007; Li et al., 2012).

claims.claim: In both PVIVIT and PIAIIIT structures, the less-conserved solvent-exposed (positions 2 and 4) and flanking (positions −1 and 7–9) residues adopt variable side chain orientations.
claims.source: In both structures, the less-conserved solvent-exposed (positions 2 and 4) and flanking (positions −1 and 7–9) residues adopt variable side chain orientations (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: This is based on analysis of published crystal structures shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Modeling approaches predicted that variations at solvent-exposed positions (V2 and V4) would have little effect on affinity, in direct contrast to experimental observations.
claims.source: All methods correctly predicted that I3 and I5 mutations decrease affinity; however, modeling approaches predicted that variations at solvent-exposed positions (V2 and V4) would have little effect on affinity, in direct contrast to experimental observations (Figure 4—figure supplement 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 5, Figure 4—figure supplement 6).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of computational predictions to experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 5, and Figure 4—figure supplement 6.

claims.claim: Only MRBLE-pep correctly discerns that a PVIVVT substitution has little effect while a PVIVIN substitution reduces binding.
claims.source: However, a direct comparison between MRBLE-pep measurements and computational predictions for two single-site substitutions in the PVIVIT motif reveal that only MRBLE-pep correctly discerns that a PVIVVT substitution has little effect while a PVIVIN substitution reduces binding (Figure 4—figure supplement 7).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of MRBLE-pep measurements to computational predictions shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 7.

claims.claim: All 4 PxIxIT peptides (PVIVIT, PKIVIT, NFATc2, and AKAP79) substantially inhibited NFAT-driven luciferase activity.
claims.source: All 4 PxIxIT peptides substantially inhibited NFAT-driven luciferase activity, confirming competitive inhibition of CN-NFAT-(PxIxIT) binding in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation from the in vivo assay.

claims.claim: PKIVIT was the most effective inhibitor in vivo, followed closely by PVIVIT.
claims.source: Consistent with MRBLE-pep measurements, PKIVIT was the most effective inhibitor, followed closely by PVIVIT.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation from the in vivo assay.

claims.claim: Co-expression of the PKIVIT peptide resulted in greater inhibition than FK506.
claims.source: Co-expression of the PKIVIT peptide resulted in greater inhibition than FK506, which interferes with CN-substrate interactions by occluding the LxVP-SLiM binding site (Rodríguez et al., 2009) and is a potent CN inhibitor.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation from the in vivo assay, with a citation to published literature (Rodríguez et al., 2009).

claims.claim: Substitution of a hydrophobic residue (IPKIVIT or LPRIEIT) at the −1 position significantly increased inhibition in vivo.
claims.source: Consistent with in silico predictions and MRBLE-pep affinities, substitution of a hydrophobic residue (IPKIVIT or LPRIEIT) at the −1 position significantly increased inhibition, whereas incorporating an acidic residue (EPKIVIT or DPRIEIT) greatly diminished inhibition.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation from the in vivo assay.

claims.claim: Incorporating an acidic residue (EPKIVIT or DPRIEIT) at the −1 position greatly diminished inhibition in vivo.
claims.source: Consistent with in silico predictions and MRBLE-pep affinities, substitution of a hydrophobic residue (IPKIVIT or LPRIEIT) at the −1 position significantly increased inhibition, whereas incorporating an acidic residue (EPKIVIT or DPRIEIT) greatly diminished inhibition.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation from the in vivo assay.

claims.claim: Introduction of the phosphomimetic mutation H9D resulted in slightly increased inhibition in vivo.
claims.source: As predicted computationally and observed in the MRBLE-pep assays, introduction of the phosphomimetic mutation H9D resulted in slightly increased inhibition; it was not possible to directly test the extremely high affinity phosphoserine or phosphothreonine in vivo.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation from the in vivo assay.

claims.claim: PKIVIT was a significantly stronger in vivo inhibitor than the previously patented PVIVIT peptide.
claims.source: PKIVIT was a significantly stronger in vivo inhibitor than the previously patented PVIVIT peptide (Nakamura et al., 2007), with activity comparable to the PKIIIT site within the known A238L inhibitor.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation from the in vivo assay, with a citation to published literature (Nakamura et al., 2007).

claims.claim: IPKIVITGPH and HPKIVITGPD variants exhibited stronger binding and inhibition than PKIVIT.
claims.source: As predicted, both the IPKIVITGPH and HPKIVITGPD variants exhibited even stronger binding and inhibition (Figure 6D); similarly, mutating the I1 and A2 residues in the AKAP79 PIAIIIT motif to create a novel PxIxIT sites with adjacent prolines and a positively charged residue in the second position (PPKIIIT) greatly enhanced inhibition.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation from the in vivo assay shown in Figure 6D.

claims.claim: Mutating the I1 and A2 residues in the AKAP79 PIAIIIT motif to create PPKIIIT greatly enhanced inhibition in vivo.
claims.source: As predicted, both the IPKIVITGPH and HPKIVITGPD variants exhibited even stronger binding and inhibition (Figure 6D); similarly, mutating the I1 and A2 residues in the AKAP79 PIAIIIT motif to create a novel PxIxIT sites with adjacent prolines and a positively charged residue in the second position (PPKIIIT) greatly enhanced inhibition.
claims.evidence: This is an experimental observation from the in vivo assay.

claims.claim: MRBLE-pep in vitro measurements were strongly predictive of in vivo inhibition.
claims.source: Overall, MRBLE-pep in vitro measurements were strongly predictive of in vivo inhibition (Figure 6E).
claims.evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparison of in vitro and in vivo data shown in Figure 6E.

claims.claim: Yeast and phage display can powerfully discriminate between 'bound' and 'unbound' peptide populations for > 10^8 protein-peptide interactions.
claims.source: Yeast and phage display can powerfully discriminate between 'bound' and 'unbound' peptide populations (Bazan et al., 2012; Cherf and Cochran, 2015) for > 108 protein-peptide interactions, and array-based methods can return information about qualitative binding strengths for many protein-peptide interactions in parallel.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature (Bazan et al., 2012; Cherf and Cochran, 2015).

claims.claim: Measuring interaction affinities for 384 peptides using MRBLE-pep requires ∼400x, ∼700x, and ∼2000x less purified protein than surface plasmon resonance, fluorescence polarization, and isothermal calorimetry, respectively.
claims.source: The MRBLE-pep assay is faster and requires less in material than alternative low-throughput quantitative methods: measuring interaction affinities for 384 peptides using MRBLE-pep requires ∼400x, ∼700x, and ∼2000x less purified protein than surface plasmon resonance, fluorescence polarization, and isothermal calorimetry, respectively, with savings increasing with library size (Supplementary file 2).
claims.evidence: This is a comparison of material requirements shown in Supplementary file 2.

claims.claim: MRBLE-pep libraries can be synthesized, assayed, and imaged in days.
claims.source: MRBLE-pep libraries can be synthesized, assayed, and imaged in days, facilitating iterative rounds of synthesis and measurement for efficient affinity landscape mapping as well as testing and refining computational prediction algorithms.
claims.evidence: This describes the speed of the MRBLE-pep method.

claims.claim: SLiM-mediated binding interactions remain statistically underrepresented in Y2H and AP-MS datasets.
claims.source: However, SLiM-mediated binding interactions remain statistically underrepresented in these datasets (Neduva and Russell, 2006; Van Roey et al., 2014; Davey et al., 2012), likely due to fast dissociation rates, and AP-MS results cannot distinguish between binary interactions and higher-order complexes, and provide no direct information about the motif involved.
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to published literature (Neduva and Russell, 2006; Van Roey et al., 2014; Davey et al., 2012).

claims.claim: The ability to return information about residues that ablate binding can significantly improve the ability to predict true targets in vivo.
claims.source: In particular, the ability to return information about residues that ablate binding can significantly improve the ability to predict true targets in vivo (Krystkowiak et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature (Krystkowiak et al., 2018).

claims.claim: This is the first demonstration that residues both upstream and downstream contribute to PxIxIT-CN affinity.
claims.source: In addition to identifying candidate peptides for manipulation of CN signaling, this first demonstration that residues both upstream and downstream contribute to PxIxIT-CN affinity redefines the motif itself.
claims.evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the findings.

claims.claim: The expanded 10-residue definition of the PxIxIT motif will significantly enhance future computational efforts to comprehensively map the CN signaling network.
claims.source: The expanded 10-residue definition of the PxIxIT motif derived here will significantly enhance future computational efforts to comprehensively map the CN signaling network, reducing the number of both false positive and false negative substrates.
claims.evidence: This is a prediction about the impact of the findings.

claims.claim: The extent of in vivo dephosphorylation has previously been shown to depend on primary PxIxIT amino acid sequence (and the associated interaction affinity).
claims.source: The ability to predict affinity based on SLiM sequence is an essential step toward accurate modeling of signaling dynamics in vivo, as the extent of in vivo dephosphorylation has previously been shown to depend on primary PxIxIT amino acid sequence (and the associated interaction affinity) (Roy et al., 2007).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature (Roy et al., 2007).

claims.claim: JNK kinase regulates CN signaling by phosphorylating a serine that immediately precedes the PxIxIT of NFAT4.
claims.source: Consistent with our findings that acidic residues at the −1 position decrease affinity, JNK kinase regulates CN signaling by phosphorylating a serine that immediately precedes the PxIxIT of NFAT4 (Chow et al., 2000).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature (Chow et al., 2000).

claims.claim: Phosphorylation of a threonine at position nine is required for binding of CN to a PxIxIT site in C16ORF74, and for its ability to promote invasiveness of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC).
claims.source: Similarly, our demonstration that phosphorylated residues downstream of the core PxIxIT sequence at position nine enhance PVIVIT affinity echoes observations that phosphorylation of a threonine in this position is required for binding of CN to a PxIxIT site in C16ORF74, and for its ability to promote invasiveness of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) (Nakamura et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to published literature (Nakamura et al., 2017).

results.result: The manuscript provides background on Short Linear Motifs (SLiMs) and calcineurin (CN), establishing that ~40% of protein-protein interactions are mediated by SLiMs, the human proteome contains >100,000 SLiMs, and CN is a Ca2+/calmodulin-dependent phosphatase that recognizes substrates via PxIxIT and LxVP motifs. The relationship between PxIxIT sequence and CN binding affinity outside the core motif has not been systematically probed.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C16 are background statements about SLiMs and calcineurin supported by citations to published literature (C1-C3, C7-C15) or established knowledge (C6, C10). Claim C16 accurately describes a gap in the field that motivates the current work. These claims provide appropriate context for the study.

results.result: The manuscript reviews limitations of existing methods for studying protein-peptide interactions, noting that display-based methods (phage display, ProP-PD) identify only strong binders and cannot probe PTM effects, while array-based methods have difficulties with peptide quality control leading to false positives/negatives.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C24 accurately describe limitations of existing methods based on cited literature (C19, C20, C22-C24) and established knowledge (C21). These claims appropriately motivate the need for the MRBLE-pep method developed in this work.

results.result: The MRBLE-pep method synthesizes peptides on spectrally encoded beads with unique linkage between sequence and spectral code, allows precise control of peptide density and PTM incorporation, has slow on/off rates enabling measurement of weak interactions, and maintains stable spectral codes throughout synthesis. Peptide density is ~2×10^8 molecules per bead.
results.evaluation: Claims C26-C28, C31-C34 describe key features of the MRBLE-pep method supported by experimental data (C33, C34) and citations to prior work (C26, C32). The measured peptide density (C34) and code stability (C33) are directly demonstrated. These technical claims establish the method's capabilities.

results.result: MRBLE-pep successfully measures CN-PxIxIT binding affinities despite prior literature showing 50-fold variation for the same substrate. High-affinity variants (PVIVIT, PVIVVT) showed strong binding, scrambled peptide showed no binding, and PKIVIT bound slightly stronger than PVIVIT. MRBLEs were engineered with slow on/off rates (hours) to approximate equilibrium, with intensities saturating at 5-6 hours.
results.evaluation: Claims C35-C45 demonstrate MRBLE-pep's ability to measure CN-PxIxIT interactions with experimental data (C36-C39, C42-C44) and appropriate controls (C37). The slow kinetics design (C44-C45) is supported by time-course data and literature (C45). MALDI confirmation of peptide synthesis (C38) addresses quality control concerns. Results are consistent with prior observations while resolving discrepancies (C35).

results.result: Systematic mutagenesis of PxIxIT core residues revealed that positions 2 and 4, previously considered degenerate, have unexpectedly strong effects on binding. V2R and V2K mutations in PVIVIT significantly enhanced binding, consistent with the high-affinity A238L viral inhibitor containing a positively-charged residue at position 2. All mutations from native R2 in NFATc2 caused dramatic loss of binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C50 present experimental findings from systematic mutagenesis supported by MRBLE-pep data (C47-C50) and sequence analysis (C46). The observation that 'degenerate' positions have strong effects (C49) is a key finding. Results are consistent with known high-affinity inhibitors (C50), providing validation.

results.result: Flanking residues outside the core PxIxIT motif make major contributions to CN binding affinity. At position -1, CN prefers hydrophobic residues (V, L, I) while acidic residues (D, E) strongly reduce binding. Phosphoserine/phosphothreonine at position 9 increased PVIVIT affinity ~50-fold, though this effect was sequence-specific. These data establish that the PxIxIT SLiM is significantly longer than previously thought.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C56 present a major finding that flanking residues contribute significantly to affinity, supported by systematic experimental data (C52, C53, C55). The 50-fold affinity increase from phosphorylation at position 9 is dramatic and well-documented. The sequence-specificity of this effect (C55) demonstrates the complexity of the interaction. This redefines the PxIxIT motif (C56).

results.result: Double-mutant cycle analysis revealed epistatic interactions between positions 2 and 4. V4F substitution reduced PVIVIT affinity but had minor effects on PKIVIT, while V4I increased binding only in PKIVIT. This suggests the high affinity of A238L's PKIIIT sequence relies on cooperativity between positions 2 and 4.
results.evaluation: Claims C57-C59 demonstrate non-additive effects between residues using double-mutant cycle analysis (C57-C58), with C59 providing a mechanistic interpretation. The experimental observations are clear, though C59 is an inference rather than direct demonstration. The epistasis finding is important for understanding binding specificity.

results.result: Comparison of MRBLE-pep measurements with computational predictions (Rosetta, FoldX) based on crystal structures showed that while all methods correctly predicted effects of conserved buried residues (I3, I5), computational approaches failed to predict effects of solvent-exposed positions (V2, V4) that MRBLE-pep showed have strong effects. Only MRBLE-pep correctly distinguished that PVIVVT has little effect while PVIVIN reduces binding.
results.evaluation: Claims C61-C62 describe structural features from published crystal structures. Claims C64 and C66 compare computational predictions to experimental data, showing computational methods fail for solvent-exposed residues. This is a fair comparison highlighting MRBLE-pep's advantages, though it also reveals limitations of current computational approaches for this system.

results.result: In vivo validation using NFAT-driven luciferase assays showed that all 4 PxIxIT peptides inhibited CN activity, with PKIVIT being the most effective (greater than FK506). Hydrophobic residues at position -1 increased inhibition while acidic residues decreased it, consistent with in vitro measurements. Novel high-affinity variants (IPKIVITGPH, HPKIVITGPD, PPKIIIT) showed even stronger inhibition. MRBLE-pep in vitro measurements were strongly predictive of in vivo inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C71-C80 demonstrate strong correlation between in vitro MRBLE-pep measurements and in vivo activity (C80), validating the method's biological relevance. The in vivo assay is appropriate and well-controlled. The identification of peptides more potent than FK506 (C73) and the novel high-affinity variants (C78-C79) have potential therapeutic implications. The consistency between in vitro and in vivo results (C74-C76) strengthens confidence in the findings.

results.result: The study demonstrates for the first time that flanking amino acids and PTMs play critical roles in determining PxIxIT-CN affinity and specificity, and identifies several PxIxIT peptides with unprecedented binding affinity. This redefines the PxIxIT motif as significantly longer than previously thought.
results.evaluation: Claims C29-C30 and C87 summarize the major findings of the study. These conclusions are well-supported by the systematic mutagenesis data (claims grouped in previous results), in vitro binding measurements, and in vivo validation. The novelty claim (C87) is justified given the lack of prior systematic studies of flanking residues (C16, C51).

results.result: MRBLE-pep offers advantages over existing methods: it requires 400-2000x less protein than SPR/FP/ITC for 384 peptides, can be completed in days enabling iterative measurements, and provides information about residues that ablate binding (important for in vivo target prediction). SLiM interactions remain underrepresented in Y2H and AP-MS datasets.
results.evaluation: Claims C81 and C83-C86 describe advantages of MRBLE-pep over alternative methods. The material savings calculation (C83) is supported by Supplementary file 2. The speed claim (C84) is reasonable given the described workflow. Claims C85-C86 about limitations of other methods are supported by citations. These claims appropriately position MRBLE-pep's contributions.

results.result: The expanded 10-residue PxIxIT motif definition will enhance computational efforts to map the CN signaling network. The findings are consistent with prior observations that JNK phosphorylation at position -1 regulates CN-NFAT4 binding and that phosphorylation at position 9 is required for CN binding to C16ORF74 in pancreatic cancer.
results.evaluation: Claim C88 is a prediction about future impact, appropriately qualified as speculation. Claims C89-C91 connect the current findings to prior literature, showing consistency with known regulatory mechanisms. These claims appropriately contextualize the findings within the broader field, though C88's prediction of impact cannot be evaluated without future work.
